claims.claim: Reviewers note that the initial experience involves sitting through lengthy cutscenes before gameplay begins.

citations.review_text: I really wanted to like this game, but I've spent about 30 mins just sitting through cutscenes, on top of that if you really want to play on keyboard/mouse you have to spend another 10-15 mins readjusting key binds. Kind of lame AF IMO. Game plays fine with  my PC specs and the graphics are pretty damn good but that doesn't make up the entry gameplay which is primarily sitting through cutscenes and for some reason they default everything like you are going to play this with a controller so you have to sit and rebind all kinds of things. If you were looking for something to just jump into and play unfortunately this has not been it...Its sad because I really wanted to like this game and thoroughly enjoyed the anime/story but I want to just play not work 40 mins to get to that point...

I don't understand why there are so many positive reviews. This game is absolute trash.

The interface and controls are terrible. You can't even properly remap some basic buttons, and the game doesn't explain its controls or mechanics properly. There's no normal story mode.. instead, you're thrown into a bunch of different missions and menus that are barely explained and often feel pointless

The game basically throws you into the action and expects you to figure everything out yourself. You collect these Arms or whatever that is and are obviously supposed to use them, but the game barely explains what they do or how you're supposed to incorporate them into combat. Even using them you see no impact anyway

Then you get to the first bosses, which are basically damage sponges with barely any mechanics, while the game doesn't even properly explain how to dodge or roll. You're just thrown into fights, taking damage, wondering what the hell you're supposed to be doing

The controls feel completely broken and unintuitive. You can't properly customize the layout, you can't configure basic actions the way you want, and the game gives you almost no useful explanation of its mechanics

Even changing the resolution is unnecessarily annoying. There's no proper list where you can simply select the resolution you want. Instead, you have to click through the options one by one and wait for the screen to update with that stupid little black screen every time. You just sit there clicking "Next" like an idiot

Overall, this has been an absolutely terrible experience. An absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game with awful UI, confusing controls, no proper tutorial, and almost no adequate explanation of how you're actually supposed to play it

I genuinely don't understand where all the praise comes from. I wish I could get my money back

[b]Completion:[/b] Full story completed, 18/55 achievements
[b]Overall Score:[/b] 8/10
[hr][/hr]
[h1]Stylish, absurd and simply fun[/h1]
Recommended if you enjoy flashy character-action combat, chasing style ranks, and a game that never takes itself too seriously.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Context[/h2]
Platform: PC
Controls: controller
Playtime at review: ~15.5 hours
Mode played: single-player
[hr][/hr]
[h2]What This Game Is in 2-3 Sentences[/h2]
Devil May Cry 5 is a fast-paced character-action game built around making combat look as stylish as possible rather than simply surviving encounters. Its three playable characters feel genuinely different, while a constant stream of new abilities, weapons and ridiculous ideas keeps the campaign entertaining until the end.

The core loop: fight through missions, experiment with weapons and abilities, defeat bosses and try to keep your Style Rank climbing.

What makes it interesting/unique: the combat rewards variety and showmanship, while each playable character approaches fights differently enough to make switching between them meaningful.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Is Especially Good[/h2]
1) The three characters all have distinct combat styles. [spoiler]V[/spoiler] was my favorite because commanding familiars instead of fighting conventionally feels completely different, but the others were interesting as well. Even though [spoiler]Dante[/spoiler] has an overwhelming number of weapons and options, you can simply find a few favorites and stick with them. The dual rocket launcher was particularly hard to put down.
2) The game has a wonderfully playful personality. [spoiler]Nico[/spoiler] constantly showing up with new Devil Breakers, the increasingly ridiculous weapons, the van somehow appearing everywhere, the soundtrack and the character animations all contribute to a game that is stylish without becoming overly serious.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Is Problematic[/h2]
1) Not every boss is equally interesting. [spoiler]Urizen[/s…

Devil May Cry 5 is an absolute masterclass in character action gaming. It doesn’t just respect the legacy of the franchise, it elevates it to near perfection, delivering a stylish, adrenaline fueled spectacle that feels incredibly satisfying to play. Instead of sticking to one playstyle, the game gives you three entirely distinct characters. Nero uses his mechanical Devil Breaker arms to grapple and control space, Dante brings his classic, mind bogglingly deep style switching system, and V completely flips the script by playing like a tactical summoner who fights from the backline. Visually, the game is a stunning achievement. The minor flaws are the repetitive environments like the second half of the game takes place largely inside a giant, fleshy, underworld tree structure (The Qliphoth), leading to a lot of visually repetitive, gray and red corridors and also V's Playstyle isn't for everyone. But if you have any love for fast paced, mechanically deep action games, Devil May Cry 5 is an essential experience.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the campaign environments feature repetitive, linear corridors and lack variety.

citations.review_text:
Devil May Cry 5 proves one thing beyond any doubt: Capcom still knows how to make combat feel phenomenal.

For the first few missions, everything looks fresh. But somewhere around Mission 5, I had a strange feeling of déjà vu... and then it happened again... and again. The environments blur together into one endless fleshy hallway where every turn looks suspiciously like the last one.

You're rarely exploring memorable castles, towers, cities, or bizarre locations like in previous games. DMC5 gives us... corridors. Combat arenas connected by more corridors. You rarely explore anything that feels distinct or alive. The game becomes a sequence of battles rather than a journey. And when the environments lack personality, even the best combat starts to feel like a routine.

Even the music starts working against the game. Tracks like Bury the Light are legendary, make you want to fight Vergil in your living room at 3 AM. But the regular combat music repeats so often that eventually it just becomes elevator music for demon slaying.

The boss fights don't help either. They're surprisingly forgettable. Ask me about Cerberus, Beowulf or Agni & Rudra from DMC3 and I can picture the fights instantly. Ask me about half the bosses in DMC5... give me a minute..

Then there's V. Every time the game switched to V, I just wanted it to switch back. His gameplay is certainly unique, but compared to the fast, aggressive combat of Dante and Nero, it completely kills the momentum.

Devil May Cry 5 is a masterclass in combat trapped inside some of the most forgettable levels in the series. The gameplay is fantastic, the old cast is as charismatic as ever, but repetitive environments and V's slower playstyle stop it from reaching the heights of its predecessors.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that starting with the Vergil mode causes players to miss out on the main story and cutscenes.

citations.review_text: If the opening scene of DMC 6 is V being destroyed: dying a horrible death that leaves no question he exists no more, I'd definitely give it a try. Being forced to play as him and even dealing w/ his dumb@$$ in cutscenes is enough to mitigate how awesome the rest of the game may be. Absolute positive if he weren't in it. Not 'not' recommending it; just get the Vergil dlc and play as him instead.

Warning for new players: do NOT start with Vergil mode.

I did, and I basically played the whole game without the actual story. No cutscenes, almost no context, and achievements didn’t track like a normal playthrough.

I thought I was playing the game normally, but Vergil is basically a separate combat-focused mode, not the main campaign.

If you want the actual game (story, cutscenes, proper progression), start with Nero/Dante/V first. Vergil is for later.

citations.review_text:
I do not understand how this game has the "overwhelmingly positive" rating - it was mid at best, boring and janky at worst.

The main thing that I disliked was how the game was actively trying pad the playtime with boring filler. Levels had long corridors with _nothing_ happening, and it felt like every 30 steps I had to watch a cutscene that could have been avoided with better level design. Fighting happens in designated arenas and is very short - I think at most I had seen maybe a dozen enemies in one such arena. It was as if the game was actively trying to avoid throwing me into prolonged fights, which is surprising as that is obviously the main attraction.
Combat was a clear example of "complexity does not make for a fun experience": there were a lot of moves bound to _extremely weird_ key combos, weird quirks and "styles," but on the "recommended for newcomers" difficulty, it all boils down to buying the dash for m1 and just spamming m1 and m2 until win, sometimes with the highest ranking. It was clearly designed for the controller, and the keyboard was an afterthought. Also, for some reason lock on must be held down instead of being a toggle like in any other game.
Full clear took me like 7 hours. It can obviously take longer if you want to do all the side content and all the difficulties as all the character, but about half way in I was just done and desperately trying to get through the slog in hopes of finding the "masterpiece" that the positive reviews keep on insisting this game was.
Outside of gameplay, the game boasts very aggressive monetization that it even shoves in your face inside the game. Very cool.

Maybe I am missing something, but to me this game came across as a very boring button masher.
In the end, the experience was barely worth the time investment (if just to see DMC franchise for myself), and given the lacking keyboard support and scummy monetization practices I am just going to give this a hard "no."

Devil May Cry 5 delivers one of the best hack-and-slash experiences ever made with stylish combat, incredible action, and outstanding gameplay depth.

Pros:

+ Extremely satisfying and fast-paced combat system
+ Three playable characters with unique fighting styles
+ Stylish combo mechanics reward creativity and skill
+ Dante’s combat depth offers huge replay value
+ Smooth performance and impressive visuals using the RE Engine
+ Excellent soundtrack that dynamically reacts to gameplay
+ Memorable boss fights with cinematic presentation
+ Strong fan service for longtime Devil May Cry players
+ Responsive controls and polished gameplay mechanics
+ High replayability through difficulty modes and combo mastery

Cons:

- Story can feel confusing for newcomers to the series
- V’s gameplay style may not appeal to everyone

Despite a few minor flaws, it remains an incredibly fun and rewarding experience. Highly recommended for action game fans — and make sure to get Vergil, because his gameplay alone is worth it.

citations.review_text:
[h1]Stylish. Over the Top. Absolutely Ridiculous.[/h1]

Devil May Cry 5 is what happens when a developer decides to make a game that is completely and unapologetically itself.

It's loud.

It's ridiculous.

It's stylish.

And it is [b]so much fun.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Music Alone Deserves a Review[/h2]

DMC5 has one of those soundtracks that makes you want to play better.

Every character has their own musical identity, and the game somehow manages to make already ridiculous combat feel even more epic.

Then Nero's battle theme kicks in.

Then Dante's.

Then Vergil's.

Suddenly I'm fighting demons like the fate of the universe depends on my combo score.

And honestly?

Maybe it does.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Style Is the Point[/h2]

Devil May Cry has never been interested in subtlety.

DMC5 embraces that completely.

The characters are absurdly cool.

The animations are ridiculous.

The weapons are ridiculous.

The bosses are ridiculous.

And the game knows exactly how ridiculous it is.

That's what makes it work.

It doesn't apologize for being a stylish, over-the-top action game.

It celebrates it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Three Ways to Be Awesome[/h2]

Nero, Dante, and V all play completely differently.

Nero is aggressive and direct.

V fights through his demons while barely touching the enemy himself.

Dante is basically an entire fighting game disguised as one character.

Then Vergil shows up and reminds you that apparently everyone else was just practicing.

There is an incredible amount of depth underneath the spectacle, and the better you become, the more ridiculous the combat starts to look.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Devil May Cry 5 doesn't try to be realistic.

It doesn't try to be grounded.

It doesn't try to be anything other than [b]Devil May Cry.[/b]

And thank God for that.

Turn up the music.

Pick a character.

Style on some demons.

[b]Jackpot.[/b]

Devil May Cry 5 is one of the best action games I have played, offering an incredible combination of stylish combat, impressive visuals, and an entertaining story. The game introduces three playable characters—Nero, Dante, and V—and each one has a completely different fighting style. This variety keeps the gameplay fresh and makes every character enjoyable to master.

The combat is easily the strongest part of Devil May Cry 5. The wide range of weapons, combos, special abilities, and Devil Trigger mechanics allow players to create their own fighting style. Dante is especially impressive because of his huge arsenal and multiple fighting styles, while Nero’s Devil Breakers add another layer of strategy. V also provides a unique experience by controlling demons during battles.

The graphics are beautiful, with detailed environments, impressive character models, and spectacular visual effects. The soundtrack is another highlight, with energetic songs that make every battle feel more exciting.

The story is engaging, and the characters are memorable and entertaining. Boss fights are challenging but satisfying, especially when you learn their patterns and defeat them efficiently.

Overall, Devil May Cry 5 is an excellent action game that rewards skill, creativity, and practice. It is highly recommended for anyone who enjoys fast-paced combat and stylish gameplay.

Pros:

citations.review_text:
"Deadweight" has gotta be one of the most successful ragebaits in all of gaming

Replaying the first DMC game I ever played after completing the rest of the (mainline) series was honestly more fun than I expected. I thought it'd be a little boring going through levels I've already beat before, but it still managed to entertain me and I found myself really enjoying myself, even more so this time around than the first playthrough.

Whilst I still think the narrative hook in 3 is better, I still feel that the final act of this game is probably the strongest the DMC franchise has been narratively, and is an incredible way to bring closure of this series (No, I don't think there'll ever be a DMC6, I don't know what they'd really do with that given where we end things off). Of course, I didn't feel as strongly about the story when I hadn't played 3 or 4, but I feel they are really necessary to appreciate everything that happens within this game.

The gameplay within 5 is also my favourite, as it takes all the fun parts of the previous games and refines them perfectly. The way they have you switch characters is so much better than it was in 4, and the difficulty of the game, whilst not as challenging as 3, is still pretty good, up until you get Dante's SDT which kinda trivialises the difficulty. I also really liked Dante's kit a lot more on a replay, as when I started out without any prior DMC experience, I found it overwhelming with all the options: 4 styles, 4 ranged weapons, and 4 melee weapons, one of which changes midgame too. This combined with the different characters who all have their own different play-styles, it's easy to see why I was overwhelmed the first time. But now with some experience under my belt and a much better understanding of how to use the game systems, it was an absolute blast.

Devil May Cry 5 delivers one of the best hack-and-slash experiences ever made with stylish combat, incredible action, and outstanding gameplay depth.

Pros:

+ Extremely satisfying and fast-paced combat system
+ Three playable characters with unique fighting styles
+ Stylish combo mechanics reward creativity and skill
+ Dante’s combat depth offers huge replay value
+ Smooth performance and impressive visuals using the RE Engine
+ Excellent soundtrack that dynamically reacts to gameplay
+ Memorable boss fights with cinematic presentation
+ Strong fan service for longtime Devil May Cry players
+ Responsive controls and polished gameplay mechanics
+ High replayability through difficulty modes and combo mastery

Cons:

- Story can feel confusing for newcomers to the series
- V’s gameplay style may not appeal to everyone

Despite a few minor flaws, it remains an incredibly fun and rewarding experience. Highly recommended for action game fans — and make sure to get Vergil, because his gameplay alone is worth it.

citations.review_text:
[h1]Stylish. Over the Top. Absolutely Ridiculous.[/h1]

Devil May Cry 5 is what happens when a developer decides to make a game that is completely and unapologetically itself.

It's loud.

It's ridiculous.

It's stylish.

And it is [b]so much fun.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Music Alone Deserves a Review[/h2]

DMC5 has one of those soundtracks that makes you want to play better.

Every character has their own musical identity, and the game somehow manages to make already ridiculous combat feel even more epic.

Then Nero's battle theme kicks in.

Then Dante's.

Then Vergil's.

Suddenly I'm fighting demons like the fate of the universe depends on my combo score.

And honestly?

Maybe it does.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Style Is the Point[/h2]

Devil May Cry has never been interested in subtlety.

DMC5 embraces that completely.

The characters are absurdly cool.

The animations are ridiculous.

The weapons are ridiculous.

The bosses are ridiculous.

And the game knows exactly how ridiculous it is.

That's what makes it work.

It doesn't apologize for being a stylish, over-the-top action game.

It celebrates it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Three Ways to Be Awesome[/h2]

Nero, Dante, and V all play completely differently.

Nero is aggressive and direct.

V fights through his demons while barely touching the enemy himself.

Dante is basically an entire fighting game disguised as one character.

Then Vergil shows up and reminds you that apparently everyone else was just practicing.

There is an incredible amount of depth underneath the spectacle, and the better you become, the more ridiculous the combat starts to look.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Devil May Cry 5 doesn't try to be realistic.

It doesn't try to be grounded.

It doesn't try to be anything other than [b]Devil May Cry.[/b]

And thank God for that.

Turn up the music.

Pick a character.

Style on some demons.

[b]Jackpot.[/b]

citations.review_text: I like Dmc 5 but this game is far from perfect. I'm not a fan with how they paced the story. V is also a blight on this game, I Hate his character and I don't like playing as him. I hope one day Capcom blesses us with a game purely centred around Dante again like Dmc 3. Because being forced to play other characters all the time is annoying. This game would've been better without V.

I really wish we had an option that can give us a mixed review on Steam, but whatever. Before I talk about this game, I want to make a reminder that I don't hate this game, but after finishing the game multiple times and going for the 100%, I can confidently say this game is slightly overrated. When I see these other reviews and hype that this game has gotten over the years, I would've expected this game to be a 8,9 or even a 10/10 game, but I only see this as a good 6 or light 7. But with that out the way, I want to talk to about the negatives that I have with this game, so lets begin.


-Lady and Trish add nothing to the story at all and are just there to be there. It's sad because I loved these ladies in the previous DMC games, but in this game, all they do is just sit and do nothing the entire game. We don't get to see awesome moments of these girls being badasses not a single time and it's honestly sad.

-V is so boring and trash to play. I like playing as Dante, Nero, and Vergil, I find those characters very fun to play, but whenever I get to play as V, I just want the mission to be over with already. All he does is sit back while he lets Shadow, Griffon, and Nightmare do all the work while you sit in the very back of the level until you get to do your finishing move. He's also very cheesy to play making it very easy for a person who has never played a DMC game to get a triple S like it's nothing.

-Another problem I have with this game is the fact you can't choose what character YOU want to play. I can understand if it was only for the one playthrough and the rest you got to play who you wanted to play on the other difficulties, but like I said before, I hate playing as V, and hopefully in the next DMC game, we rather have this option where you can play as any character on any mission after we beat the game or just make it where every character is fun to play.
